title: Why (non-const) global variables are evil
recap: A non-const global variable creates hidden shared state: any function with access can change it, so callers cannot understand behavior from a function's parameters and return value alone. This increases coupling and makes defects harder to trace.
Prefer local variables and pass required values as arguments. When one mutable resource truly must be program-wide, hide it behind a narrow interface rather than allowing unrestricted direct access.
objectives: Keep mutable inventory state local to main.
Pass values explicitly into a calculation function.
Return a result instead of mutating hidden state.
Demonstrate that the same function works with different arguments.
warnings: A naming prefix makes a global recognizable but does not remove its coupling or mutation risks.
Avoid global variables that control decisions, because an unrelated call can silently change program behavior.
Objects with static storage duration in different translation units can also introduce initialization-order hazards.
challenge: Implement remainingStock as a calculation over its stock and shipped parameters, with no mutable global state. In main, keep the starting stock of 18 and shipped count of 5 local, calculate the remaining stock, and make a second call for a 9-item sample with 2 shipped to demonstrate reuse.
hints: Give remainingStock two int parameters rather than reading any file-scope variable.
Return stock - shipped without changing either argument.
Initialize local constexpr inputs in main and print results returned by the function.
